_notes.sources: FY2023-2024 adopted budgets, US Census ACS 2023, Lincoln Institute Land Policy, ICMA, IndyStar, individual city budget documents. All figures normalized to general fund equivalent where possible. Per-capita uses most recent Census population estimate.
_notes.methodology: Public safety = police + fire + emergency dispatch. Parks = parks, recreation, open space. Human services = housing, community development, social services, health (where city-funded). Admin = finance, HR, legal, clerk, mayor/manager, IT. Infrastructure = public works, engineering, planning, streets. Pension and debt service excluded from category percentages where separable. Some figures estimated from published budget summaries.
_notes.caveats: Direct comparisons are imperfect. Some cities include utilities in GF, some fund transit through GF. Indiana cities use township assessors; others don't. College towns have unusual daytime population spikes that affect per-capita figures. Use as directional context, not precise benchmarks.

cities.name: Bloomington, IN
cities.note: 2026 adopted budget. Public safety share is unusually high relative to peers — 57% of GF. Parks includes seasonal staff.

cities.name: West Lafayette, IN
cities.note: FY2024 budget. Lower human services spend reflects reliance on Tippecanoe County services.

cities.name: Muncie, IN
cities.note: FY2024. Higher public safety share reflects higher crime rates and older population. Parks notably underfunded vs peers.

cities.name: Columbus, IN
cities.note: FY2024. Strong parks investment relative to size thanks to Cummins Foundation contributions to public space.

cities.name: South Bend, IN
cities.note: FY2024. High public safety share. Mayor Pete Buttigieg-era investments in tech/innovation less visible in GF.

cities.name: Fort Wayne, IN
cities.note: FY2024. Economies of scale visible in lower per-capita GF than smaller Indiana cities.

cities.name: Evansville, IN
cities.note: FY2024. Highest public safety share of Indiana peers. Parks and human services squeezed significantly.

cities.name: Indianapolis, IN
cities.note: FY2024 consolidated city-county (Unigov). Largest city in Indiana. Includes county services in GF equivalent.

cities.name: Iowa City, IA
cities.note: FY2024. Strong parks and human services relative to peers. Lower public safety share than Bloomington despite similar size.

cities.name: Lawrence, KS
cities.note: FY2024. Lower per-capita GF reflects Kansas property tax limitations. Infrastructure share higher than peers.

cities.name: Champaign, IL
cities.note: FY2024. Most comparable in size and character to Bloomington. Higher police staffing per capita.

cities.name: Ann Arbor, MI
cities.note: FY2024. Lowest public safety share of all peers. Highest parks investment. Strong human services. Often cited as model progressive city budget.

cities.name: Boulder, CO
cities.note: FY2024. Highest per-capita GF of all peers. Lowest public safety share. Extremely high parks/open space and human services investment. Outlier — very high property values drive revenue.

cities.name: Madison, WI
cities.note: FY2024. Larger college town. Strong parks and human services. Often compared to Bloomington as progressive Midwest peer.

cities.name: Minneapolis, MN
cities.note: FY2024. Post-2020 budget debates significantly reduced police share. High human services investment. Parks funded separately via Park Board.

cities.name: Austin, TX
cities.note: FY2024. High public safety share despite large progressive movement. Texas cities face significant public safety salary pressures.

cities.name: Portland, OR
cities.note: FY2024. Lowest public safety share of major city peers. Highest human services share — reflects significant homelessness response investment.
